blocks.text: **The problem.** You are given an array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order. Remove the duplicates **in place** so that each unique value appears once, keeping their order. Return `k`, the number of unique values; the first `k` slots of `nums` must hold them. What is left after those `k` slots does not matter.

blocks.alt: The sorted array [0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4] becomes [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, …] with k = 5. The first five slots hold each value once; the rest is ignored.

blocks.text: The array is **sorted**, and that changes everything: all copies of a value sit next to each other. So a value is new exactly when it differs from the value just before it — there's no need to remember every value you've seen.
"In place" means you overwrite `nums` itself instead of building a second array. The judge only looks at the first `k` elements, so you never have to clean up what comes after them.
Put every value into a set, then write the set back in sorted order.
This works, but it uses **O(n) extra space** and ignores the one fact that makes the problem easy: the input is sorted.
The key insight: keep a write pointer

Use the same reader/writer idea as in **Move zeroes**. `write` is where the next new value goes, so `nums[write - 1]` is always the **last value kept**. `read` scans forward; when `nums[read]` differs from the last kept value, it's new — copy it to `write` and advance.

blocks.alt: Snapshots on [1, 1, 2, 2, 3]. The read pointer compares each value with the last kept value at write − 1. Duplicates are skipped; new values are copied to write. Green cells are the kept values.

elements.text: 2 ≠ last kept (1) → copy it to write
elements.originalText: 2 ≠ last kept (1) → copy it to write

elements.text: 3 ≠ last kept (2) → copy it to write
elements.originalText: 3 ≠ last kept (2) → copy it to write

blocks.text: At the end, `write` is exactly the number of unique values — so it is also the answer `k`.

blocks.alt: Using a set: O(n) time and O(n) space. Write pointer: O(n) time and O(1) space.

blocks.text: One pass, one comparison and at most one copy per element: **O(n) time, O(1) extra space**.

items: **All unique** — `[1, 2, 3]` gives `k = 3`; every value is copied onto itself.

blocks.text: Where this idea shows up again

A popular follow-up allows each value **at most twice**. The only change is the comparison: compare `nums[read]` with `nums[write - 2]` instead of `nums[write - 1]`. The same pattern also merges runs, compresses repeated characters, and removes a given value from an array.
